utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Everyone is here except Mr. Meek and Mr. Bourgon, as previously recorded. Prosecution, it's Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Thayer. Good morning to you, Major.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer will be proceeding and concluding with his examination-in-chief and then we start with the cross-examinations. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Major.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Before we resume where we left off, in reviewing your testimony from yesterday, I just noticed one thing at page 4808, line 7 to 9, and I just wanted to make sure that the transcript reflects accurately what your response was. The question I put to you, at lines 4 through 6, was, "I want to turn your attention briefly to the actual VRS attack on the enclave. Did you have an opportunity to see what was being struck by the shelling?" And the answer as reflected in the transcript is, "Yes. Warehouses around the compound itself, what was in our line of site, and it -- warehouses near, for instance, Budak hill that was on the opposite of the compound." I just wanted to verify with you whether that is an accurate reflection of what your answer was intended to be.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No. That's not an accurate reflection because I was -- I have said that there were houses that had been struck by shelling and not warehouses.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you say houses, what are you referring to, just regular houses?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Regular houses where the people lived in near Budak hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. What I'd like to do is, rather than mark up further the exhibit from yesterday, which was getting a little crowded, if we could be shown a clean version of 65 ter 1522, please. And do you have an image on your screen, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, I have an image.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You have the stylus in your hand, I see. Would you please mark with an A the location of the woman you saw who made the sign across her throat and showed you the direction towards the location where you eventually found the bodies?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Okay. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And would you mark with a B, please, where you saw a Serb soldier chasing a woman out of an area of some houses, please.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you testified yesterday about the APCs that were in the area on the 12th and were they in the same -- well, were they in the same area approximately on the 13th as you recall?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, they were in the same area.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And would you circle that on this photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And would you just write APCs next to that circle.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if you would, would you draw a rectangle around the area, that you recall on the 13th, the remaining refugees were, as they waited to pass through that APC blockade?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if you just write "refugees" next to that as well, please?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, Major, yesterday you referred to an area, or more specifically, a line of buses along which you saw Serb soldiers separating Muslim men after the point where Lieutenant van Duijn was active. Would you please just draw a line or maybe an arrow along the area that you were describing to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: For the record, that is two arrows extending downwards on this image.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think if you would just, please, initial the image anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Major. And we can save it now. Major, did you see any force being used on the refugees as they were being directed to or placed on the buses?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Initially, when they left the area behind the APCs where the line was drawn by the Lieutenant van Duijn, then the people start walking towards the buses and then when it wasn't going that fast enough sometimes there was -- there was someone pushed in a bus or were getting instructions in Serbo-Croatian, very rude instructions, but not that much violence.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you see any kicking or hitting in addition to the pushing or did you only see pushing?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Only pushing, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I want to turn your attention to the last area I want to cover with you this morning. Major, do you recall the portion of your Krstic testimony I summarised yesterday, in which you were shown a photograph in which you recognised a Serb soldier whom you described in your words as not being a plain soldier. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what you meant in your testimony in Krstic by those words, "Not a plain soldier"?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Not a plain soldier, it's quite obvious that when you're on the ground, who is in charge and not. There is a sense of authority to the officers and the NCOs in the area because they know what to do, they are well instructed, and that's the way you can distinguish the people who are on the ground. And it was very clear to me that there were a certain amount of Serbs that were in control, although they were not wearing any insignia, but also T-shirts and other gear and other clothing, but it was very clear to me that they were in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, specifically with respect to this individual whom you identified in the photograph, can you recall anything about the way he was conducting himself that led you to draw the conclusion that he was not, as you said, a plain soldier?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: He was -- he gave them direct instructions to other Serb soldiers. They were speaking to him. There was a way of contact, what is also normal in our army, that there is a certain distance between the men on the ground and between the NCOs and the officers on the other hand, so you can always tell who is in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, can you recall what kind of uniform this soldier was wearing and/or any insignia at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: They were wearing also camouflage uniform or a camouflage trouser with brown and green T-shirts.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, but with respect to this particular individual, do you have any recollection, as you sit here today, of what that soldier was wearing when you saw him outside the "White House"?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: The moment I saw him outside the "White House", he was wearing camouflage trouser and he had green/brown T-shirt.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, I want to show you an image. We are going to do it from Sanction, just to advise the Trial Chamber, because if we do it through e-court, there is going to be some identifying information underneath it and we wanted to crop that out, so it's simply the image. So if we could see 65 ter number 1936. This is chapter 5, page 9. Sir, do you have an image on your screen?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, I have an image.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And was this image shown to you during the Krstic trial?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes. Also, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: As you sit here today, do you recognise the man on the right in the camouflage shirt?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise him.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall seeing the man on the right during the 12th and 13th in or around Potocari and do you recall also seeing other photographs of that man?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just generally, would you describe for the Trial Chamber the role that you believe that the man on the right played at the time, as you had an opportunity to see the man on the right in the green camouflage shirt?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: It was clearly that -- that he was the man who was -- who gave the instructions and who was very clear to me that he had the authority and he was in charge over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, as you sit here today, Major, do you recognise the man on the left in the brown T-shirt?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And whom do you recognise that man being?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: I don't have a name, but I saw the man also near the "White House".

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And is this the man that you had described previously and that we have just been discussing, who was somebody that appeared to you to be not a plain soldier?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes. That's the man also.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, is it fair to say that on Monday night, you had to be reread a portion of your Krstic testimony in order to refresh your memory of that man on the left?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And prior to reading that testimony again, is it fair to say that you weren't entirely sure that you recognised that man on the left?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the objection?

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to my learned friend cross-examining his own witness as to -- in my submission, this is a proper matter for cross-examination, not to ask his own witness these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you wish to comment on that, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm simply placing in context the current testimony. I think it's relevant evidence. It's appropriate to ask this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't agree with your objection, Ms. Condon. This is the normal progression of the examination that Mr. Thayer has been conducting and seeks to further explain and -- illustrate his position in relation to this photo. So go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: My last question, Major, and I think you've already answered part of it, but to this day, do you know the name of either of the men in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Major. I have no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Thayer. I take it Mr. Josse is going first?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We've agreed to go first, Your Honour. That's right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Josse, together with Mr. Krgovic, Defence counsel for General Gvero, and he will be cross-examining now. How long do you expect to be, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: About half an hour, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Major Rutten, as a member of Charlie Company, were you aware of the theft of any of your weapons prior to the events that you have been describing yesterday and today?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes. In the evening, before I heard from other soldiers of the company, that there already were weapons been taken by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So we are talking about July, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yeah, July, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My fault. I didn't frame my question carefully enough. Prior to July?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Prior to -- okay. Then that's a different question, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Indeed my fault. What's your answer to that.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Not prior -- prior to July, there were no weapons taken from our company and not from the battalion that I know of.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So you've got no memory or knowledge of the company being overwhelmed by about 30 or 40 Muslims and taking some of your weapons?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No knowledge of what whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could speakers please not overlap.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My fault again, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We speak the same language, Major. Of course, there are translators. I need to go much slower.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that on the 10th and 11th of July, at all material times, you were in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, I was in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And the journey that you have described to Srebrenica, was that on the 13th of July or sometime before that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: If you mean the journey that was told yesterday in the late afternoon of 13 July, then it was on the 13th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And so you were also in Potocari throughout the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In those three days, that is the 10th, 11th, and 12th of July, did you see any resistance at all from Muslim soldiers or irregulars or indeed any form of resistance whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Not on that spot. Not on the spot of Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Where did you see some resistance?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Not actual resistance, but during my journey, as you asked before, in the evening of the 13th, to Srebrenica, I -- on the road to Srebrenica, I saw a group of Bosnian soldiers, Muslim soldiers, who were hiding in a house. I stopped there and asked them whether they -- what they did over there because it was quite dangerous to be around there. And I suggested to them that they get the hell out of there because they could be getting in a problem. As I drove away, and I was only a few hundred metres further down the road, my car, my jeep, was hijacked by Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That was, as you've just said, on the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: For what it's worth, my question referred to the 10th, 11th and 12th. So perhaps we could just concentrate on those three days, first of all. You saw no resistance at all from Muslims during those three days?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Not in my line of sight near Potocari, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You were in a bunker for some of that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yeah, during the morning sometime, but I wasn't often in the bunker. I was one of the men who wasn't sleeping in the bunker because I saw no use of sleeping in the bunker. I was sleeping in the shelters that we had to [indiscernible].

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I agree that when you were asleep, you wouldn't have seen anything any way, but how many hours did you spend in the bunker on each of those dates? Can you assist?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Altogether, a few hours, I think, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want to take you, on this subject, to an answer that you gave when you were being examined in chief during the course of your evidence in the trial of General Krstic. And at page 2109 of that transcript, Mr. Harmon, prosecuting, said this to you, "Captain Rutten, you've described heavy shelling in the Srebrenica enclave. Can you tell me, based on your presence on patrols and your experience in the enclave, were there any military targets in the town of Srebrenica or in the town of Potocari?" And your response was, "There were no real military targets. The military targets that were there were on the confrontation or border line at the time of the enclave. There were some BiH soldiers still but not in Potocari or Srebrenica itself." Now, I have a number of questions about this exchange between you and the prosecutor in that case. Firstly, he says to you that you've described heavy shelling in the Srebrenica enclave. Your description related to what was going on in Potocari and no where else; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: There is a difference between --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, one moment. What's the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just to clarify, Your Honour, when my learned friend refers to your description, I just wanted to make sure we understand whether it's his description that he gave here or the description that he gave in the Krstic trial, that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fair enough. I think you can address that, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My question relates to the question that Mr. Harmon asked you in that trial. And, in particular, the words that he used. And I suppose what I'm asking is what you understood by them, because he says, I quote again, "You've described heavy shelling in the Srebrenica enclave."

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: My describing was quite clear then because, at that time, I had two radios on me and I could hear every report that came out of Srebrenica area, because the Bravo Company was acting in that area and I had that -- that on my radio as well, so that I could read every radio signal that came through about -- in the southern part of the enclave. So also the reports on the shelling, I heard on the radio. So if you referring to my statement then, then it's referring to that situation by the radio transmissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, that clarifies that, and it's right to say that what you actually saw and heard with your own ears, so to speak, was what was going on in Potocari, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I now want to turn to your answer to Mr. Harmon's question and I read it once and, if need be, I can read it again, but you said there were no real military targets. Now, I don't want to be facetious about this, but what would you describe as an unreal military target?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: An unreal military target, it's quite clear to me that are civil houses as I described before on Budak hill, that are civilians walking around, that is shelling where there are no real BiH soldiers around and there weren't any at the time, only a few wounded ones. So that to me are not real military targets and there were no BiH positions near the Potocari area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And so your use of the word "no real military targets" refers, as you just said, to -- and let me get this right, a reference to civilians who may have been perceived as a military target?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: There weren't any civilians who were wearing, as we describe it in our humanitarian law that we use and it's also reflecting the international military law, wearing suits that you could see that they were military personnel around. So there were just civilians around wearing normal civil clothes and if I refer "no real military targets," there were no manned positions in -- near the Potocari area of BiH soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Although I think at another point in your testimony in that case, you mentioned an encounter with a BiH soldier that you knew from your patrols, who had civilian clothing on; he wasn't in military fatigues. Do you remember mentioning that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. And that was the piece that you already also read, the man in the wheelbarrow, and I knew him because I have seen him before during patrolling and he was wounded then, he had a shot wound, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I think you understand that the commented to that Trial Chamber, that you didn't blame him for wearing civilian clothing, you would have done the same in his desperate situation?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's right. So would it be right to characterise him as a soldier who had put on civilian clothing?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. You described, not I think in the course of that testimony, but in one of your briefings, I can take you to it if need be, that as you have described it, armed men took leave of their wives. I think you were referring to the 11th of July. Do you remember ever saying that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And -- well, perhaps you could describe that to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes. That was on the back side of the compound. It's even on the image we have on my screen here. I can point it out to you if you want to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Can I stop you because I am going to ask you in the course of my cross-examination to mark a plan, but a different plan to the one you've got there.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Perhaps up on the screen, P10516 [sic] can be placed. It's wrong on the transcript if the transcript is being relied upon. It's P01516. Yes. That's it. You may want to take a moment to orientate yourself. It's a very similar shot but of course covering a larger area to the photograph you were previously looking at?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I'm going to invite you to be given the stylus and mark this in a number of ways. Perhaps you could begin then by marking the point that you say the armed men took leave of their wives.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Okay. It was at the -- this is a small stream down here and here, in the corner, we made an entrance in the fence. It was at the opposite side, there was a small bridge at the rear side of the -- of our compound and this was our compound, with the factory hall in the middle, large factory hall, and at the back side, we call that our -- of our compound, made an entrance, and here at opposite side it was a small bridge, and at the -- the other side of the stream, and that's exactly here, there were some BiH soldiers greeting their families and the wives and the children were put on the -- on our compound, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what number of men would you say were involved in that encounter, armed men?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Three.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Three, that's all?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I see. And these people had come from Srebrenica, presumably?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: I can't tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Then changing the subject slightly, I want to suggest to you that looking at this map, the vast majority of the refugees took the road that is visible in the north of this map. Although rather confusingly, this map is actually upside down, so that the north is in fact the south but I'll call it the north, coming from somewhere near where the Z and the E of Herzegovina is.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you agree with that, that that is the road where the majority of the refugees streamed down from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes. I agree on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I want to suggest to you that somewhere down that road, there was a -- there were scenes of men and women separating, the women coming towards the Potocari base, the men going to the right, as we look at this photograph.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: It is a little bit different than you -- than you describe it, because what I described as the stream, we were getting the -- a lot of people inside our compound in the cover of the trees around the stream. As you speak about the vast majority, that there were around the former bus compound, and that is here, and I texted it on this area as well and the majority of the refugees, as I stated yesterday also, were in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. We are agreed on that, by the way.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Okay. Then if they came down with the line of buses, then you could see on this image as well. Most of the refugees were travelling like -- on this side and another part of them, mostly the separated ones, were travelling on this side. And where the separation -- wherever it took place along this line, the men and boys were taken out of this group of refugees and were being brought or sent to the houses that were along the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We may be at cross-purposes. You are talking about the separation of the men on what date?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: It already started on the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Okay. Perhaps it's my fault. I was asking you about separation, if it happened, between men and women, on the 11th of July, as they left Srebrenica. The Serbs were not there at that point, at the point that I'm asking you about. They hadn't arrived, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: You're right on that. There wasn't any separation on the 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And my question is this: The point that you've marked on the plan where the refugees came from, do you recall a natural, for want of a better word, a natural separation taking place between men and women, with the women coming into the base, eventually through the hole, and the men going to the right as we look at there photograph?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No, there was no distinction on that as you call it, natural, and certainly not on the 11th, because there was no separation whatsoever on the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: At that time, we agree, there were no Serbs in the vicinity?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, we agree on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Where did the Serbs eventually arrive from?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: If you mean eventually, on what date do you mean? On the 11th or the 12th?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You were there. You tell us.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: On the 11th, we -- there weren't any Serbs around then. On the 12th, it depends, in the morning there was already reported from the south they were coming in and during the later morning, they came from all kinds of sides. They came in from the north. We got the report from the direction of OP Papa. They came in from the south as well. We get a reports from the rest of the B Company. And they came in from, so to say, the Quebec and Romeo area for us, and that is this area. They came here from the hills down, and at this point where I put that arrow, that was my line of sight, and they came out of the hills over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, I want to initially ask you about the Serb forces that came from the north, which, as we both agreed, is at the bottom of this photograph, in other words, from the Bratunac area. Were you aware of any resistance at all at the bottom of this photograph, from Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that and there was nothing report on -- on BiH resistance at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Because I want to suggest to you that there were some mortars at the bottom of this photograph trying to repel Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: That could have been, but I was regularly in the days before and also on the 11th, on top of the factory hall where there was a post of 108 company -- 108 platoon Commando Company and there were no, at that time, no signs of BiH mortars around. The only thing that we saw from the top of the factory were in the hills of Purici, Serb positions with mortars and even a tank that they drew -- drove out, in and out of their position, intimidating us, because they saw us on top of the factory hall and we saw them in the hills of Purici.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When you were carrying out these observations, do you remember which members of your company you were with?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: That were -- was no one of my company was around on that. I was alone on the roof, together with them, the man that I recalled, a Lieutenant, and a few men of 108 platoon, on the top of the factory hall. And later on there came also the -- our surgeon, a Colonel Kramer on top of the factory to watch what was happening in Purici hills.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Prior to the Serbs arriving, do you remember any Muslim men fleeing from the vicinity? In other words, trying to avoid capture.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: On the 11th, I was outside with Lieutenant Koster during the day and we had a report that the -- at the entrance of the compound, that there were two soldiers. They waved with something. We got the report. So that was one of the moments I was in the bunker and we got that report. We went outside at the gate to check what that was because they were reported as probably a BiH commanding officer. But as we came at that point, and I shall point it out to you, that was here was our entrance, and the soldiers here was also a building and they were behind this building, two men, but the card that they had was a card that was on his arm and there was a wounded card which was filled out by one of our soldiers on -- from OP November. I could read his sign, his signature on that card, who had helped the man. The man had a gunshot in his underarm and that was it. We gave him some water and we send them back because we -- we didn't want -- we didn't want have BiH soldiers near our compound because it could have been that then the Serb forces would identify that then as a BiH position. So that could attract attention and even fire so it could be dangerous for civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What I want to suggest to you is this: That there were Muslim fighters who fled prior to the arrival of the Serb forces, or at the time of the arrival of the Serb forces, to the upper right-hand part of this photograph. What do you say about that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: In the evening on the 11th, there were reports from former and even then also actually working with us, laundry women from the Muslim people, and they told me that the men, Muslim men, were fled to the, as we call it on the maps, the Buljim area, that's between OP November and OP Alpha, to get out of the -- to get safely out of the enclave area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could you mark that area, please.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: It's not -- I can only give the route to that Buljim area, but the route to that Buljim area was between those bushes you see here and it's in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. And am I right in saying that that is basically leading to Jaglici and Susnjari?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Josse, because I don't want this to escape us later on. In line 9 on page 20, previously in line 6 of the same page, the -- whoever is in charge of the transcript did not catch the word, the name that the witness mentioned. We are talking of the Buljim, Buljim. Yeah. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, it's being helpfully suggested to me that I need to invite to you mark the map with some of the things that you have indicated. It might be worth starting with the hole in the perimeter fence.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I mean an H for hole would do, I think.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yeah, okay. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The large marked area top middle of this particular photograph, perhaps an R for refugees, if the Trial Chamber are content with that.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The line to the left, the arrow to the left, I think represented incoming Serb forces; is that right? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Perhaps SF for Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And the two lines to the right of the photograph, would you be content to mark MF for Muslim fighters?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: The problem is --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: The thing that I reported just right now that were not only soldiers but were men leaving and you're now saying to me that they were Muslim fighters leaving.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Absolutely. I'm not trying to make a cheap point. MM, Muslim men, would be fine.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Okay. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you a little bit about your discovery of the bodies, and in the course of your testimony in General Krstic's case, which you have adopted in this case, you say that your discovery of those bodies took place on the 13th of July; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As far as you can recall, Major, have you always been consistent about that discovery taking place on that date?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Because I'd like to - without being too dramatic about it - confront you, as lawyers sometimes say, with a previous statement of yours, and this is 3D46. If that could be put up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm told what's on the screen will need to be preserved, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, we need to save that first.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So could you sign that, date it, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Bottom right, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's the 30th of November.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. Whilst this is being put up on the screen, the information I have been provided with about this document, it's described as a Dutch MOD debriefing statement dated the 23rd of July 1995. I don't think we have been provided with a Dutch version, and I'm not clear whether the document you're about to look at is in fact the original. So that's one of the things I'd like to ask you, please. We see that it's got -- bears your name, and we see the date that the interview was conducted, and it says, "I am co-coordinator for Srebrenica. On the morning of 11th July 1995, there was a rumour in the local refugee camp that seven people had been shot and the bodies were near the well in Potocari." You then describe knowing the area well, driving to it with Messrs. Koster and van Schaik and you saw a man running in that direction, also a woman, and you then discovered nine dead men who appeared to have been shot lying face down. So my first question, if I can break this down, is perhaps you could help us as to what this document is.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes. I can help you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: The last ten years almost, but not the last two or three years, it became quite quiet in Holland about this affair, and you're laughing, but it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Only to be fair, it's in response to your --

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: It's laughable to other ones, but not to us. And the reason why I'm saying this is the following: During that so-called debriefing session in Assen, all soldiers, and that you will find that in the NIOD report as well and in the other reports, and in the parliamentary inquiry, had enormous problems with this debriefing statement in Assen, because they were never signed by us, they were rewritten, and the problem that we had with it was that a lot of our messages that we tried to bring over, we never found back in our statement that was put down during those days. So if you're referring to this document, this worthless piece of paper, if I call it like this, and then, yes, feel free to do that, because that's the only thing I can say about it, and you will speak to some other colleagues as well about this -- these statements, and almost no one of my colleagues is -- stands fully behind those statements in the debriefing session that was held in Assen in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: A few follow-up questions, if I may. Firstly, --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment before you do so. I just want to confirm something with whoever. The English version that I have, indeed at the end of the statement, just states, end of interview. There is no indication of who the interviewer was, any signature, just the top, the interviewee and the date of the interview. Can I see the end, please, of the same document in Dutch, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I observed, there isn't one in Dutch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm seeing it on the screen. I have it on my monitor. Oh, I see, I see, this is B/C/S, I see. Okay, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd rather my learned friend didn't comment at this stage and I'd rather ask the witness. And perhaps after I've asked the witness, I would be happy to hear some information thereafter from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You can address the witness on this but I just want to make sure if we can have available a Dutch -- the Dutch copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was the exact question I was about to ask him literally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we need to see it if it is available.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Absolutely. In fact, the question I was about to ask you, Major, is are you aware, is there a Dutch version of this available or was this interview conducted in English, the statement written in English? Can you help us.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: It was in fact -- in fact, it was in Dutch as I recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So do you think this is a translation or was the report of the interview, so to speak, written in English?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No, it was a Dutch version, I think, and there was no reason to put it into English because it's a -- it was a Dutch matter, as I said before.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Absolutely. Well, Your Honour, I've asked the question. Any help from my learned friend would be gratefully received on our part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. And perhaps we can also ask the witness himself whether he has a copy of this so-called statement, as he wishes to describe it, in his own language. You have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you happen to have it here with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Two issues, Your Honour. I'll take the most recent one first. With respect to this one page interview document, we do not have it in Dutch. The only copy, the only version we have, is in English. That said, I also want to clarify, I think, a misunderstanding between the witness and my learned friend as to which document we are talking about. The document I believe, as my learned colleague has identified, that is on the screen, is a Zagreb debriefing document that was taken while the DutchBat soldiers were in Zagreb before they returned to Holland where they were again debriefed in what we now refer to as the Assen debriefing. So there were actually a series of debriefings, if you will, beginning upon their immediate return or their immediate stayover or layover in Zagreb. That is what we are being shown here on the screen. And I believe what Major Rutten has been referring to is actually the subsequent Assen debriefing. So we are a little bit at cross-purposes. The Assen debriefing, we definitely have in Dutch, that's been furnished to the Defence as well as the B/C/S translations obviously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I think we need to confirm or modify this statement of -- by Mr. Thayer. Major -- shall I take it over or would you like to address this having heard Mr. Thayer yourself, because we need to eliminate the possibility that we are talking of two different --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm grateful to my learned friend, but I was, in fact, going to deal with those very matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then go ahead. I will not interrupt you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Major Rutten, you've heard what Mr. Thayer, for the Prosecution, has said. Is it right that you were interviewed in Zagreb on the 23rd of July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And in the answers that you were giving me earlier, was there any confusion on your part between your debriefing in Assen and your interview in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No. I always stated the same dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So you were aware that this particular interview was conducted in Zagreb that resulted in this particular document, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: I got that document far more later, the real copy of it, than at the moment in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This document?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Any idea when you received it?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No. I can't recall that. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you, on receiving it, complain to the -- your military police or someone in authority that this was a misrepresentation of the facts?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No. I never did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: There was no reason for me, because all my other reports that I -- that I did and that I worked with the military police were correct and these reports, yeah, that I -- much more later I got this one. So there wasn't at that time -- there was no reason to correct it because I simply hadn't the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We've now clarified that this took place in Zagreb. Perhaps you could tell us about the circumstances of those interviews. Are you as critical of the way they were conducted as you are of the way the Assen interviews were conducted?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Because it wasn't a real interview with a direct report, as I stated before, and you never got the chance to sign the report and to read it over before you sign it. So -- and if you never get a copy, and the conditions in Zagreb where they held those interviews with us were quite typical, as I -- were quite typical because there were only questions and nothing was written down directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sorry, what do you mean by your use of the word "typical"?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yeah. That's difficult to say. There is -- there was a certain disbelief by me at that time what they tried to achieve with those interviews with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your evidence to this Chamber is that you never said the 11th of July. Is that what I'm understanding you --

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- to assert?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And that this is some horrible mistake?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: I don't know who draw this statement, who drew the statement, sorry, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Not much more on this. When you were interviewed in Zagreb, tell us briefly, if you can, about the procedure. Were you interviewed alone or were you interviewed in the company of other DutchBat members?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you recall how many interviewers there were?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: There were two opportunities, because I reported myself in Zagreb. Myself, I wasn't asked for. There was an interview with a human rights personnel there and there was an interview with the chief in command of the army that I spoke then that particular morning, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If I suggest to you that it is a possibility that you discovered these bodies on the 11th of July and that this first statement of yours was correct, what do you say?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: I'm not agreeing on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: One other aspect of this document which I think, in fairness, you confirmed in your later testimony. You say that there were rumours of these killings in advance of your discovery of the bodies. Were the rumours circulating, to the best of your knowledge, on the day of the discovery or sometime prior to that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: It was on the day of the discovery, and there is something else I want to say about the 11th. On the 11th, we weren't outside the compound because on the 11th, that was the particular day that we cut the hole in the fence. On the 10th, in the evening, we made the first beginning of that and at the 11th, we finished the hole, we enlarged it, waiting for the refugees to come in, waiting for the order to be given by my superior to let the refugees in. So if there ever has been written by someone 11th of July, it is simply not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So you are sure, in fact, it was two days later, the 13th of July, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And on the 11th of July, there were no Serb forces. And I'd suggest to you, you were quite free to patrol the area safely at that juncture. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No. That isn't right because you're rephrasing things and you're getting things out of the context. Because at the 11th, there was still shelling in that lane from Purici hills down towards Potocari. So at this moment you won't be hearing me, but this is -- yeah, might be something different. But when I'm speaking to someone, it's polite that he listens to me and otherwise, I -- because you put your headphones off. So did you listen, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Rutten, I apologise, but I have an advantage, which is I'm able to follow the transcript in English. I was taking some instructions from my lead counsel in this case, asking him whether I should ask you any further questions. I don't mean to be rude to you. And though I'm not the learned Judge in this case, and he can control the proceedings, I would suggest you just answer the questions and let me worry about conducting my own case. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And I think I have to endorse what Mr. Josse stated. Please try to avoid any across-the-table confrontations between you. Everyone is doing his or her job here. And let's kill it here. Major, could you kindly answer his question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could he rephrase his question again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sure Mr. Josse will oblige.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The question was simply whether -- I suggested to you that it would have been quite safe for you to go out and patrol that area in Budak hill on the 11th of July because there were no Serb forces in the vicinity.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: My answer to that is that is not correct, because also in the evening on the 11th, one of the APCs, the medical APC went out and came later on in from Srebrenica, and was shelled when it came in, and also some cars from our battalion. So -- and the shelling came from Purici hills. So it wasn't safe then to do any foot patrolling at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My last question or set of questions to you goes back to the document still on the screen, 3D46. Prior to giving evidence in this case, in other words, yesterday, had you looked at that statement again? In other words, over the last few days, have you had a chance to re-review that particular statement?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When was the last time you think you saw that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. Who is next?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, how long do you expect your cross-examination to last?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: 30 to 40 minutes, Your Honour. I know I indicated approximately 15 yesterday, but in reviewing some of the documents, I believe I can complete it within 30 to 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are not going to restrict any of you and that's because this particular event, the nine bodies, there are so few witnesses available that I think it's only --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- chance to deal with these witnesses as thoroughly as possible. So Mr. Ostojic is lead counsel defending Colonel Beara in this case, and he will be cross-examining you next.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Major Rutten.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will have a break at 10.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to ask you a little bit on the follow-up questions that you were just asked specifically in connection with this worthless piece of paper, and where in your opinion, a paper should be given to you, a statement, where you sign it and then read it or read it and then sign it again. I don't necessarily disagree with you, sir. And I'm going to show you an Exhibit which is 3D37. And with the usher's assistance, if we could look at the last page of that document which has the last three ERN numbers 326. The last page of that document. Thank you. Sir, this is basically a witness acknowledgement form which clearly sets out, and I'm sure you've read it, which clearly sets outs that you've read the statement and you read it in your own language which would be the Dutch language, and in fact that it's true to the best of your recollection, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yeah, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: This is the type of statement that you were referring to when you said or when you were critical of some of the Dutch Defence Ministry's interviews or debriefings that you were -- had in August of 1995, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So this statement, if I tell you was taken approximately in October 9th, 1995, that would also be near or about the time of the events and that would be something that would be closer to your recollection than ten years later, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, could have been. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember giving a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on October 9th, 1995?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And if we look to the first page of this document, it's actually the witness statement -- acknowledgement is attached to that very document, October 9th, 1995. You see that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yeah, I can see that. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now preliminarily, I'd like to ask you first, who is Petrus Hendrikus Rutten?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: When you -- my name is on top of that, Johannes Hendrikus Antonius Rutten, that's my name.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I understand. But who is Petrus Hendrikus Rutten?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: It's a MP officer of the Netherlands royal mounted police here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Any relation to you, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No. No relation, but I do recall the name, because he is the man who did the investigation in the Kodak team when I came back in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, you had given several statements, including the debriefings, and just to highlight them, you gave one on the 23rd of July 1995, as we discussed or you had discussed earlier, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You also gave a statement on the 6th of September -- I'm sorry, on the 2nd of August 1995, to this Mr. Rutten with the military police, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And then your third statement would have been the second debriefing with the Defence Ministry on the 9th -- on the 6th of September 1995, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And then your fourth statement in 1995, would have been this OTP, as I call it, witness statement that's before us, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, am I correct that on July 11th, 1995, that initially it was DutchBat who planned not to allow men into the compound?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Although -- okay.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Correct on this?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. One moment. I'm sorry to butt in but Major and Mr. Ostojic, particularly you Major, please allow a very short brief interval of time, brief pause between question and answer because when you overlap, the interpreters will have problems and I have a duty to protect them. So, Mr. Ostojic and Major.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It was my fault, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's okay. I am sure you will comply. It happens even sometimes with me but --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In fact, sir, it was your decision on the 11th of July to let some men in the compound to stay with their families and you particularly, sir, made the decision to allow the men into the compound who were obviously not armed, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me take you, sir, to a topic that we have discussed here a little bit and that is screening of military men as combatants. Do you, sir, agree with me that it was quite clear that there was a selection that was made of certain men who were suspected of being combatants by the Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, so when you -- is it obvious also to you, sir, that that was what was going on?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: I don't understand your question, because at what point do you mean what was going on?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, that's fair. Thank you. I'm talking about on July 12th, 1995. Wasn't it rather obvious to you, sir, that the selection process or the screening had been made of certain men who were suspected of being military combatants?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, there were -- sorry, yes, there was a certain screening going on, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, it was -- what a made it so obvious, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: What made it so obvious? The first thing I saw that it made that obvious and then I'm speaking about the 12th, was that they -- they looked at hands of BiH people, civilians, and they had a -- quite a selection on age, but I -- it was very hard for me to understand that the boy from 12 years until 15 years and some I asked for their -- for their age, that they could have been soldiers, combatants, and there were men that could barely walk. So if that are combatants, then, okay, we have a new kind of army then.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, let me ask you: Other than checking their hands, what other things were done in this selection process of certain men?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: There wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: On the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: On the 12th of July, the selection process was merely that -- that almost all men, for exception, real elder men who barely couldn't walk, were sent to the houses on the line that I draw that -- that I drew this morning, and even the boys, as I told you before.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, let's take a look at your statement, sir, on the -- I think it's the third page, which ends in ERN number 322, if I may. Again, sir, we are referring to this statement that you read in your own language and that you signed, October of 1995. I just needed you to clarify a couple of things for me. We will take that first paragraph. It says, "On Wednesday morning July 12 or 12 July 1995," do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And towards the bottom or the end of that same paragraph, you have this sentence that we just covered, these last two lines. It says, "It was obvious by then that a selection had been made of certain men who were suspected of being combatants," correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, my question to you, when you say "certain men," that doesn't mean all men, does it?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No, that doesn't mean all men.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And the certain men is some men, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: That is some men, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And the men that were actually being selected or screened on the 12th of July 1995, were men, as you put it, who were suspected of being combatants, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, let's go to the next sentence there. You give us the similar or the same example but you preface it by saying "among other things" and you state, "Among other things, men were checked for fingers smelling of gunpowder." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What other things, sir, other than checking the fingers of those -- some men who were suspected of being combatants were they doing in the screening process?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Looking at their clothes, looking if they had ID or weapons on them, and then they were sent to the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that was it, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: That was it, but the problem is, and that rose my attention, that the age of the men that were sent to the houses was not the age of the men that we should see as combatants.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, is there defined in the Royal Dutch military certain ages when a person can be identified as a combatant in a civil war?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: We had never a civil war, so that's difficult then but we now, boys from 17 years old on, we take in for a first year of more or less school training. So international rule says, below 18 years, you cannot have boys on a battlefield or as combatants. And I stated just before, and I want to emphasise that, that when there are pupils around in a house where I made photographs, then I can no longer say that they are or could have been combatants.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We will get to those photographs in that -- what did you call it, a house?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Didn't you call it though an interrogation house in some of your earlier statements?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, I called it an interrogation house.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You called the area where you inspected an interrogation area, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. We will get back to that. Now, sir, if someone, hypothetically, like the Office of the Prosecutor and a member thereof, states in their opening statement that there was no screening, based on your testimony and your recollection, and the statement that you gave, they would be incorrect; correct? And just for the Court, it's page 426, line 15, the 21st of August, 2006.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: The screening that I meant there and that's words are being rephrased and were taken out of context, I think, is that a normal procedure for combatants, and I mean combatants in a normal situation, as we train our soldiers, is that we do a specific check on ID, on weapons, on a lot of things, and then we -- we label them, more or less, to clear whether they later on, to get the belongings to the right persons and that the right person has a number, and we do that with envelopes. But the situation in the so-called interrogation area was merely dropping their belongings and their IDs on a huge pile in front of the "White House".

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, we'll get to the interrogation in a minute and I know you're anxious to get to that. I'm asking you this, sir. If the Prosecutor, on the 21st of August, 2006, said, "No screening," that would be incorrect?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yeah, that would be incorrect, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, let's talk about interrogation. The first time that you had seen any interrogation in this "White House", as you call it, the interrogation house, was the next day, the 12th of July, 1995, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And, sir, in that house, wasn't it true that it was your opinion that you could hear voices and that the voices implied normal conversations were going on, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, if there was no interrogation, why would you identify or coin the "White House" on the 13th of July when you visited it as an interrogation house or as an interrogation room or area, as you have done in your statements?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: The reason we said that was that there were a lot of men going in, and eventually, and I can't tell if all had been interrogated at that time, but a lot of them went in a separate room and been interrogated or at least there was a conversation going on, as you mentioned it, in that room, but I couldn't see what in that room was actually happening because I was not allowed to go in that room.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, you could hear -- you could hear actually what was going on in the room, sir, couldn't you, and you could in fact hear that there was no screaming and that there was no sounds indicating any maltreatment; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: The moment I was in the house, that -- I was trying to get an overview of what was happening there. When I was in the entrance of the house, I only stood for a few moments in the -- in that entrance, and later on I went up the staircase. So it wasn't a situation, to put the whole situation in the right context, that I could listen up quite nicely, lean through the door and hear very nice what there was going on. It were just fragmentations of information that I could pick up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well let's take a look at the next page of your statement in October of 1995 that was read in your language and signed. I think it ends in ERN 323. Sir, I'll represent to you, although we can look at the page prior, just so you know, we are talking about the 13th of July there, and it says it on the page prior, but just for the benefit of this quick question before the break, if I may, hopefully, you'll except my representation. It states there in the fifth or sixth line there, "I could hear voices from the room. These voices implied that a normal conversation was going on. I did not hear any screaming or any sound indicating maltreatment." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Earlier in your answer to me, you mentioned "we", but actually you in October of 1995, when you gave this statement, you specifically remembered this and it was your opinion, sir, specifically, that the voices implied that there was nothing wrong going on in the room. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: That was correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, I see that it's 10.30, but I would like to finish this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you formulate an opinion at that time that the Serb soldiers simply wanted to find out whether there were any Muslim soldiers among the men in the compound?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: It was -- you make a connection there that isn't there. And it wasn't my opinion at that moment as well. My opinion at that moment was that there was something going on, I was inside the house, the connection that you made with men that were on our compound is a totally different one. At the moment I was at the "White House", I was investigating what was happening over there, and my first view in the entrance of the house, and that's already clearly stated, was that there was someone hanging a few centimetres with his feet from -- on a staircase. So if we speak about that, and if I speak a few moments later, about a situation that I could see no maltreatment by hearing a normal conversation, then it's only a selected moment at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to be unfair to you, sir, but we'll go through that, that comes later in your statement.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What I'm asking you directly, which is the next sentence in your statement, and it's my opinion, sir, and you tell me if I'm correct, that it was your opinion that the Serb soldiers simply wanted to find out whether there were any Muslim soldiers among the men and that was why they were interrogating them in this interrogation house or interrogation room or area as you put it; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And, in fact, that's specifically what you say in your statement, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes. THE INTERPRETERS: Could the speakers, please, slow down and not overlap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's time for a break, Mr. Ostojic. Let's have a 30-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me just give some brief information before we start. After the next break, we'll be sitting without Judge Kwon, who cannot be with us. Monday, we start at 10.00 and not at 9.00 and then tomorrow we are not sitting, you know that, and Friday week, we will not be sitting either, on the 8th, we will not be sitting either, so please make note of this. All right. And incidentally, while we are at it, as well, you asked for a week in February for reorganising your ranks. That will be a week which starts on the 12th. 12th February, of course, yeah. All right. 12th February, Monday through Friday. Okay? That will be off, as per your wishes. Then you had asked for the week starting on the 26th of March. We are unable to give you that. However, we have agreed as follows: That in the following week, the week which starts, if we say that the week starts on Monday, the week that starts on the 2nd of April, we will sit from Monday to Wednesday, and then we will not sit from Thursday, which is Maundy, Thursday, 5th April, right through Friday, the -- and inclusive of Friday, the 13th of April. So the week you asked for before, we are giving it to you after instead. All right? And that's because of other exigencies that the Trial Chamber has and organisational priorities. So if you want further clarifications on this, if we haven't been clear, please, let me know and I'll come back to you. Sorry, Mr. Ostojic and Major Rutten, but if we don't do these things now, they might escape through the back door and will not be able to catch up with them. Yes, Mr. Ostojic, go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Major Rutten, before the break we were discussing your first visit to the interrogation house, I believe on the 13th of July, 1995, and I want to ask you, sir, if at that time, there were any Dutch soldiers in the interrogation house?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: At the time there were already two soldiers posted already by a colleague of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
