utterances.text: And I've been specifically, I don't want to say warned, but told to stop. And I apologise if I've spoken too fast to the interpreters and to you, sir. I'll try my best to slow down the questions. Who were those two soldiers, those two Dutch soldiers?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: They were two soldiers of 108 platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: As you sit here, sir, do you know their names?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, after you left the interrogation house on the 13th of July 1995, I think, at least according to your statement and what I've heard in your direct examination, you were told by some interpreter that there were several bodies or seven or so -- nine bodies that were found in a meadow, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And can you tell me, sir, the next time that you went to the "White House" or interrogation house, when was that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: That was after that I found the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Was it the same day, the 13th of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And it was several hours later, possibly?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, several hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, at that time, sir, you also went back to the interrogation house and you saw that the Serb soldiers were holding Muslim men for interrogation, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And at that time, sir, was your estimate that there was approximately 3 to 500 Muslim men in the house?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yeah. I stated 300 at that time, because the house wasn't that big to hold 500 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know in your prior statement if you've ever given an estimate that was higher or lower than that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No, it's -- by my knowledge now, it's always about 300.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, were those two Dutch soldiers from the 108th --

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: -- company, thank you. 108th company, were they also still at the "White House" when you returned on the 13th of July 1995, for a second time?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yeah, they were still at the "White House" and not any more inside the house, because they had given a message that they had to wait outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, is it fair to say that you, at that second visit on the 13th of July, were trying to arrange the release of those men in the house?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: If we speak about the release of the men, the second time I was in the house, I saw a more or less total filled-up house and we were the only ones that were bringing water in. And I saw an almost inhuman situation down there and I spoke with some colleagues at the main entrance of the compound, and that was Warrant Officer Rave, and an UNMO named Major De Haan, a Dutch one, and I said that we should do something about that situation at the "White House". There was also an UNMO around called Kingori, that was an African colleague, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you at any time, sir, speak to any Serbian leaders regarding the evacuation of those Muslim men?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Not that I can recall of, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Perhaps your statement of October 9th, 1995, would refresh your recollection on that. So if we can look at the next page ending -- again it's the same exhibit, but ending in ERN 324, which is 3D37. Thank you. We have in front of -- the second visit on the 13th of July, 1995 to the interrogation house where you came back, and prior to that paragraph that you see, you see the reference to nine corpses above that. So I think I'm accurate in this being the second visit, but you correct me if I'm wrong. Sir, I'd like to focus your attention on the middle portion of this document or your statement where you state, "My impression was that the evacuation of some would not improve the situation, but as it was, the situation was untenable." You proceed, sir, to say as follows: "I then went to see one of the Serbian leaders and told him that he ought to arrange something for the evacuation of the Muslim men." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Does this refresh your recollection, sir, that in fact it was you who sent to see a Serb leader, as you put it, and you told him that he needs to do something to arrange for the evacuation of the Muslim men from the interrogation house to some other area?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: As I see it, yes. I spoke with -- there were -- I'd rather put it like this: There were a lot of conversations going on throughout the days. It's difficult to say what you've said each specific moment, and it's quite semantic now to see your own words drawn out of a context. But then, again, I spoke to Serbs about the unbearable situation in the house of the men and I said what can we do about it to -- to put this to a better situation. But if I used the word "evacuate," to evacuate the men, I'm not sure, and I am well aware of the fact that I, in this statement, this word is used, but at that time, for me "evacuate" meant going into custody somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In fact, the word evacuation doesn't appear just in that sentence, sir, that you gave, when you gave the statement to the Office of the Prosecutor that you've read in your own language, that you signed. It appears also in two lines above that, does it not?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You consistently in this statement, sir, had you not, used the word evacuation of the Muslim men, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, and it's -- sorry, sir, that I interrupt you but --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Quite all right.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: -- we use in the Dutch military, and even in the -- with our NATO colleagues, EVAC as a quite common word. So if we speak about words now, and that's the thing we're doing here, I think -- for instance, if we have a wounded man and we want him out very quickly, we call that a CASEVAC with helis. So using words in the military -- yeah, vocabulary, more or less, seems something different than to the civilian vocabulary and that is something that we should take in notice, I think, because I was speaking then in -- on a military facility with military colleagues to a well known private investigator, I know, from the UN. But then, again, the word evacuate we do use in the military with another meaning than in civilian life.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I wasn't really focussed that much on that word evacuation. However, I don't want to take anything, sir, that you say out of context, so please forgive me if I do. I'm merely reiterating some of the things that you said and I'm trying to refresh your recollection that it was you, sir, who went to the Serb leaders and had talked to them and in fact arranged for their to be an evacuation or a transfer of Muslim men from the interrogation house to some other area; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the name of this Serbian leader or leaders that you spoke to?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And in fact, sir, isn't it also true that the Serb military complied with your request and, in fact, because of your request, they got buses organised so that they could move these men from the interrogation house to another area, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: That is a conclusion that you are drawing now. I'm not drawing that conclusion, because we saw later on the day buses coming or were actually there and getting the men out of the house into the buses. But if this was the result of my conversation as a lieutenant to the Serbs is something else. That is a conclusion that you made there, and I'm not -- yeah, I'm not affirmative on that, if I can put that on that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let me show you how I reached that conclusion, sir.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: After you state in your statement that you read an in your language that you signed confirming that you spoke to Serb leaders and told them they should arrange something, the very next sentence, sir, that you write, and that you told the Prosecutor you state, "The Serbs arranged for two buses to be driven to the house."

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's the very next sentence, is it not?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, it's the very next sentence, but this is an overview of what happened during a complete day, and it doesn't mean, if it is the next sentence, that it immediately happened afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But it happened, in any event, after you spoke to those Serb leaders and seeking them to arrange transport or evacuation or any other word or adjective you want to use, after you spoke to these Serb leaders to get the buses, that's when the buses came to transport or evacuate these Muslim men from the interrogation room; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: You're also, again, drawing the conclusion that my question was being -- was being held by the Serbs to do that that way, and I -- I don't see that like that way, because they did nothing we asked for, so the buses could have been planned already. That is also a conclusion I could draw out of this text. So again, I'm not agreeing with you when you draw this conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I don't believe that I'm the only one drawing the conclusion, sir. I think it's plain in your statement. Can you point out in your statement, sir, where you state anywhere or in any of the statements, those that you endorse, those that you don't, the following: "That I don't see it like that way because they did nothing we asked for, so the buses could have been planned already." Where in your statements, four in 1995, one in 2002, and I believe another one in 2000, where have you ever said or reached that conclusion, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: The question was never asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you this: Do you know, sir, as you sit here, and do you recall, that after this discussion with Serbian leaders and after the buses arrived to evacuate the Muslim men from the interrogation house, did you not know, sir, that they were being taken to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, because that same morning, a lieutenant also escorted buses in the direction of Bratunac, but I wasn't aware of the fact that this -- of these buses were also going to Bratunac. It was unknown until that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay, well let's look at the next paragraph of your same statement where you state, "The men from the house" -- let me stop you there. That's the interrogation house we are talking about, right?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: "... filled the buses and I think there were 60 to 70 of them in each bus." Then you proceed in the very next sentence to say, "I heard later that the men were taken to Bratunac." Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, I don't want to unreasonably conclude anything, sir, but isn't this statement that you gave actually concluding that those men who were in the interrogation house on the 13th of July, 1995 were put on buses and from what you heard taken to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: That's correct, if you put it like this, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, let me ask you in your role as an intelligence officer in Srebrenica in July of 1995, do you learn of any information where people were trading or illegally profiting from what was known as a black market at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: There were some rumours but we had no concrete evidence on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you, sir, as an intelligence officer and as a policeman and platoon leader, did you conduct any investigations in connection with that black marketing?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: I have to correct you. I'm not from a [indiscernible] intelligence officer but an infantry officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: That's the first one. And I'm not, certainly not, a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you conduct any investigation, sir, of this purported black market?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And why not?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: There were some rumours and everything we, from the company, had and rumours were put in reports to the battalion and the battalion was in the lead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, we spoke a little bit about screening and I think I have your testimony on that. I want to talk, again, just briefly about interrogations, if I can. In your statement you mention interrogations on several occasions during both visits to the interrogation house and in other statements you do as well. Would it be unfair, hypothetically, for the Prosecutor, on the 21st of August, 2006, given your statement, which was signed, under oath, which you've read in your own language, to say, "That there was no interrogations to speak of"?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Now, I cannot -- I cannot state this kind of putting it, because -- this way of putting it, because there was a -- and maybe I'm wrong by putting it like this in English, but there was certainly an interrogation going on during my visits to the "White House".

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think you put it quite well, sir. Let me ask you this: In your statement to the royal military police in south Holland, you -- it states as follows on page 18, which is -- let me get that exhibit for you, which is 3D41. Sir, in this statement, is it true, on page 18, that it was you and the Dutch soldiers, specifically, Sergeant Major Rave and others who arranged for the transport of buses having the Muslim men transported in the direction of Bratunac? Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No, that's not accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you see it on the statement that's on the e-court, page 18 of your statement? It says, first paragraph, "We arranged for transport by buses together with Sergeant-Major Rave of the I," probably standing for intelligence and "V," apparently referring to security section, "two full buses were the first to leave. The Muslim men were transported in the direction of Bratunac." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That statement is incorrect that you gave to the Dutch royal military police?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No. That statement isn't incorrect but I spoke to Sergeant-Major Rave and the UNMO De Haan who was also there at that time and we discussed the situation in the "White House", and as a result, subsequently, buses came and were driving towards Bratunac. But if this was the immediate effect, that is something that is, again, I think, it is stated there, but it's out of -- if you put it like that, it looks like if it is out of the context of what was really happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the date of this statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I have that date, Your Honour, although I don't see it right on there. I think it's the 6th of September -- I'm sorry, the 2nd of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And where was it taken?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It was taken in Holland from my understanding, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If I just may correct my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: South Holland in the Zeeland district, it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The date of the overall report that was filed by this so-called Kodak team was the date cited by my learned colleague, however the date, as we can see from page 15 of the actual interview, I believe, is 28 July. I just wanted to correct that for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And on the 28th of July, where would this interview have taken place?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The front of the document indicates --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the witness can --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we can look at that first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If he can remember. It was the 28th of July, where would you have been interviewed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was in Arnhem in the centre of Holland.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm asking you because, before we had another one, which I think also carried the date of the 28th of July and it was in Zagreb, when -- yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: 23rd of July, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. When did you leave for good the territory of ex-Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We came back on the 21st of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which complicates matters. If you came back on the 21st of July, how could you be interviewed in Zagreb on 23rd? I'm not trying to create problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Speakers, please, not overlap.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could just ask the witness to break down where he went after he left the DutchBat enclave on the 21st of July, I think it will be made clear. And I tried to do that earlier, but I think, out of the witness's mouth, it will settle the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you for that. Will you take care of this, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll try, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Major Rutten, there is a little confusion on the dates. If you can tell us to the best of your recollection when it is that you left the enclave in 1995?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: It was on the -- the date is difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: But we came back in Holland on the -- on a Monday. That was clear to me, but I don't have the calendar of that period of time exact in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me just go through just a couple of the statements so that we have a clear record with the court's permission. Sir, it was our understanding that you gave an MOD, which is an a Ministry of Defence debriefing interview, on the 23rd of July, 1995, that I think has been identified as being in Zagreb; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yeah, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Approximate dates, those are the dates we see on the interview?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Then following that, sir, it's my indication that you gave or were interviewed by the Dutch military police on the report on Srebrenica sometime thereafter with the report being dated the 2nd of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yeah, that's correct, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And then a month or so later, on the 6th of September, 1995, you gave a second debriefing statement to your Dutch Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's also right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And then approximately a month thereafter, you gave the 9th of October, 1995 statement to the Office of the Prosecution that we previously saw, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Van Hecke, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may just proceed on a different issue maybe?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: This Dutch military police report, do you remember reviewing that, sir, and signing that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That also is a report that you had an opportunity to change or modify if you felt that what they were recording was inaccurate; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now we spoke a little bit about your quote where it says, "We arranged for transport by buses" and I think you challenged or you mentioned that it may have been taken out of context. If we can just look at page 17, to look at the context in which you were describing that you, sir, or you and your Dutch soldiers arranged for the transport of these Muslim men from the interrogation house. And we'll get that up in a second. Page 17, do you see that, the last paragraph. It talks about the second visit to the interrogation house on the 13th of July, 1995. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In fact, it follows almost similar to your testimony of the individuals who were there, the estimate of the number of Muslim men that were in the house; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I don't want to take it out of context, but it seems to me that it's in the proper context. Not only did you, sir, speak to Serb soldiers or leaders as you put it in your October statement, you, sir, yourself, with your men, in fact, arranged for buses to have the Muslim men transported to Bratunac; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: It looks like if we were in control to arrange that. That wasn't the case. We weren't in control.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, tell me this: Did any Serb soldier, as you identified him as a BSA in your statements, did they ever stop you, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well look at your statement in that same paragraph, page 17, where you state, "I was not stopped by the BSA." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, but by entering the house and entering the facilities near the "White House", but I also, in -- was stopped and that is also in different statements, when I tried to get in the orchard behind the house, for instance. So I'm not saying that you are lifting it out of the context, but I'm saying --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: -- what I'm saying is that it looked like here that everything happened subsequently after each other at that moment. But it changed from situation to situation, from position to position, where I was, during those days. So if it was put in any statement somewhat different, then in a previous or in a previous statement or later on in another statement, yes, it can be the case, yes, because in that situation during the last days in the enclave, there happened quite a lot and this is an understatement if you know what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I think I do, sir, and I appreciate that. Sir, not only did the Serb soldiers not stop you from going into the "White House", you were allowed and you were able to speak to the Muslim men, were you not?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's all the questions I have, Your Honour. Thank you very much. Thank you, Major Rutten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ostojic. Who's next is Madam Nikolic. How long do you expect to cross-examine this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 15 to 20 minutes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. We'll have a break as usual at 12.30. Then today we will be stopping at 1.30 and not a quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I need to correct the transcript. I am defending Drago Nikolic and not Major Nikolic from the Bratunac brigade concerning whom you testified. This is a correction in relation to the transcript. Now, let me ask you something about what you testified on pages 17 and 18 of the transcript, when the army started entering Potocari. You said that they came from all sides, from a number of observation posts and that they were pouring down from the hill towards Potocari. Earlier in the Krstic case, as well as yesterday on page 42, whereas in the Krstic case, it is transcript page 2117, you testified that among the first soldiers who entered were the soldiers of the Rambo type; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: That is correct. That would on the side of the bus remise or compound where I was at that time, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please speak into the microphone. Interpreters have trouble hearing her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic, the interpreters have asked me to draw to your attention to try to speak into the microphone as much as possible because they are having problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe it should be better now.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could you please describe in greater detail what you meant when you said that those soldiers were more or less of the Rambo type? Could you please describe to us what that unit looked like?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: They were wearing also camouflage trousers, at least, some of them wearing T-shirts, some of them wearing also camouflage jackets. They had bandages around the head. They were wearing knives, large knives, on their belts. And it is not only what they looked like, but it is the way they react. I asked them not to go into the area of the -- of the red and white tape that we drew around the bus remise, but they simply went in and they did what they had -- think that they could do there because we marked that area as a UN area where refugees were being held. And -- but they took simply no notice of what I was saying there. So that that is, if I said Rambo types, that means that they were very offensive way of, yeah, walking around, do as they please in that area, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: So we could say that they were acting in a completely undisciplined way, in an arrogant way?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Undisciplined, I cannot say, because perhaps that was the orders they had been given, but at least arrogant, yes, sure, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You also spoke to us about the nine bodies that you found near a stream. You mentioned that on pages 46 and 47 of yesterday's transcript and you also mentioned it today when cross-examined by my colleagues. Let me ask you this: How long did you remain in that location, when you reached the stream near the location where the bodies were, where you were with other colleagues?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: It's a matter of minutes. We came in in the meadow, we saw the bodies. As I told this morning, I examined them, what was happening. I told the colleague to pick up the IDs or passports or working permits or everything that was laying around there. I checked the bodies. I checked each one of them. And I asked my colleague to pick up the IDs, the sergeant major van Schaik, and I asked Lieutenant Koster then to sit among -- in the middle of the bodies, wearing his UN cap. The reason was that -- and make a photograph. The reason was that I then would later on say that we were present as a matter of a -- or as a clear evidence that we -- what we saw that moment, just an objective view of what we found there in that meadow. And it happened in a few minutes more or less, because the moment that we were there, some shots were heard and there is a difference between shots overhead or nearby, and that was shots nearby. So we had immediately after that had to leave the meadow and as the story tells, we went back to the road again.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That means that you were unable, nor could you afterwards, conduct an investigation about this event?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: It was a -- I wouldn't call that an investigation. It was just a checking what was happening over there. I looked specifically at the bodies. There were two that were laying on the side and the rest of them were laying on front, on the front side. It was near to a small stream, a very small stream and the meadow and it was clearly that they were shot there on the spot. And that is if you can call it an investigation, it was a very short investigation what was happening there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I would agree with you that it was just a brief analysis of the situation. My question was whether, on the following day, or later that day, you conducted any sort of an investigation. Was it possible at all for you?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No, it wasn't possible because we couldn't cross the line. We were not able to walk around freely because the Serbs were not -- were not allowing this to us any more. So we had no freedom of movement whatsoever. So it wasn't possible to investigate it furthermore.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: This means that you don't know who is responsible and you don't know how these people were killed?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: I don't know who is responsible, no, because I wasn't an actual witness at that moment, but how they were killed, they were -- that was -- is also in my statements, I think, and there was -- there were wounds of small arms calibre weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just to clarify, for the sake of the transcript, something that is not contentious between the Defence and the Prosecution, in the Krstic case, when you testified about Major Nikolic, who was the liaison officer of the army of Republika Srpska, you actually testified about the gentleman called Momir Nikolic from the Bratunac Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions. Thank you, Mr. Rutten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Nikolic. Who is going next? Mr. Lazarevic, who is appearing for accused Borovcanin, will be cross-examining you next. How long do you expect to be cross-examining the witness, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning. How long do you expect your cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the cooperation of the witness, if we don't enter into some serious disagreements, I believe that I will make it in an hour and a half. I was trying to formulate my questions in the way that the witness could simply answer with yes or no, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Major. During the proofing for your testimony, you met with Mr. Thayer or some other representative of the OTP. On that occasion, you most likely -- actually, not most likely, you confirmed this yourself, you went over the transcript of your testimony in the Krstic case. Did Mr. Thayer or whoever proofed you at that time show you the other statements that you gave?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All of the statements you gave, be it in Zagreb or in Assen or statements given to the military police or to the Dutch parliamentary commission, I'm now referring to all of the statements given by you.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: We went through the binder of statements, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And when you went over these statements, I assume that took quite some time. Did you draw attention of Mr. Thayer to any of the details that were not sufficiently precise or incorrect in your statements?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Now you're presuming that I'm -- go over the statements if it was a kind of a homework for me. And if you put it like that way, I haven't gone over them that specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Actually, my question was: Did you say to Mr. Thayer, "Look here, I noticed some of the things that are not correct in some of the statements, at least the ones that I checked in detail"?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: There were -- we had a discussion of a -- there were a lot of statements throughout the last ten years, and there were some statements, as I stated before, that, like the Assen debriefing, where I had some problems, but -- with it, because -- because they weren't signed or they were rewritten or whatever, but we didn't went over in detail that specific statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can I interpret your answer to mean that you never said to Mr. Thayer, "I noticed some things that are not logical"? Did you, for example, point out to him that the statement was not signed or anything else that you just said to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No, because as I said before --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't want you to gain an impression that I'm interrupting you while you're answering. I'm just trying to abbreviate the procedure. If you can just say no, I didn't say that, or yes, I did say this to Mr. Thayer, because you've given an explanation earlier. Now I'd like to turn to the statement that we've already seen in e-court here. That's the statement you gave to the OTP on the 9th of October, 1995. This is Exhibit 3D37 in this trial. I assume that you went over that statement very carefully, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: You gave the statement and signed it at the time. It was read out to you in a language that you understand, and according to the best of your recollections, is it correct and specific, precise?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: If you mean the statement that -- with the interviewer Jan Van Hecke?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The statement you have on the screen before you dated 9th of October, 1995. Yes, Jan Van Hecke. That's the one I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Unlike the statements that you spoke of, which you provided under substandard conditions and never signed, did you encounter any problems when giving this statement to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: This statement was already in the hands of OTP. So we spoke about it, but not in specific detail, as you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. We'll leave this for the time being, this topic. This statement, page 2, last paragraph, on page 3, first paragraph, you say that the refugees started arriving in the early afternoon on the 11th of July, 1995. Is that consistent with your recollections?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, that is consistent.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We received certain information here in this Tribunal, according to which, on the 11th of July, 1995, members of the Dutch Battalion urged the population of Srebrenica and surrounding settlements to set out towards the base in Potocari, to leave their homes because the Serbian army was approaching. Did you witness this yourself?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So you can confirm the fact about the Dutch soldiers issuing appeals to the people from Srebrenica to leave their homes and go to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Now you're saying something else than before. If you're saying issuing appeals, the population was on the run because, from the south, the Serbs were coming in, so they looked for safety. And they were simply from out of Srebrenica asking on to members of the B Company to find a safer place. So they went, at first, by themselves and later on B Company, the commander of B Company, issued a guidance by some DutchBat troops to -- on the road to Potocari. But there was no appealing, as I know of, from DutchBat soldiers to go to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Listening to your evidence now, I could see that you said, as far as I know. Does this mean that you do not rule out the possibility that this were such situations or do you categorically rule that out?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: I cannot answer that with yes or no, because it isn't something that belongs to my knowledge of that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right, Major. Even if you tell us, "I don't know," that's a completely valid answer. In your statement, you said that initially you were not going to let the men into the compound, into the base. I assume you meant the men who had arrived with these refugees at the base. What was the reason for that, for not allowing men into the compound?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: The reason is it was simply not possible to check everyone who was coming on to the compound, if they were -- if they were having anything that could be threatening to our company. That's one. Or to our battalion. And the second thing is, and that was the orders that were given also, women and children first, as you know what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I fully understand you. It seems that you are anticipating some of my questions. However, did you receive a specific order, "Do not let the men into the compound"? Did you, yourself, receive such an order or did you know of anything issuing such an order?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: We only got an order to let women and children in and not the men.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Who issued that order to you?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: The company commander of the staff company was the first one who came up with that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you give us his name, if you know it, so that we can compare it with other data that we have?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: That was the Major Otter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On that occasion, when such a large number of refugees started arriving at the Potocari base, you told us that there were soldiers among them who started saying goodbyes to their families, and you concluded that on the basis of their military-style uniforms and the weapons they had that you could clearly see; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes. I stated before that there were three soldiers saying goodbye to their families at the rear side of the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: You could clearly see that they had weapons on them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: If we go further through your statements given to the Office of the Prosecutor, at one moment you let into the compound men who wanted to stay with their families and who apparently were not armed. That was your testimony to the investigators of The Hague Tribunal. That is contained in paragraph 1 of the page -- of page 3 of this statement. Do you recall letting a certain number of men, who wanted to stay with their families, into the compound?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes. If we speak about men, then, that were very young men, or very old men, who weren't able to do any duty or active duty as a combatant.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: May I understand your present answer as testimony that, in the Potocari compound, there were no men who would be able-bodied in terms of an age-appropriate for military service?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: If you say no men, that is not correct, because the Major Franken also permitted a certain amount of men inside the compound who were -- who could have been active combatants but they were more or less let in as speaking men towards the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, it seems that we have some problem with translation. I was warned by interpreters. Could you please repeat the last portion of your answer here. You said, "They were more or less let in as speaking men towards the Serbs." That's what we have in transcript and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As I understand it to be spokesmen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go-betweens between DutchBat, the Muslim population, and the Serbian authorities. That's how I understood it to be. But I agree the translation is poor in there, yeah.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay, you're very correct, there, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Does that satisfy you, Mr. Lazarevic? Is it clear in your mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That's it, because I have to admit that I was warned by the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I saw something strange too, but I more or less I was understanding what's beneath.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Major Rutten, here you stated that you let a certain number of men who were not armed into the compound, and then you said that you could not establish whether they possessed anything that could jeopardise the safety of DutchBat members. So does this mean that you frisked or searched the people who were entering with their families, going through their pockets, their rucksacks? Did you make sure that they could not carry into the compound pistols, hand grenades, knives, something that could be easily concealed?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No. I was not able at that time to do that, a thorough search, but the men that came in, as I stated before, were older men, younger men and also a lot of men who were badly handicapped, so we didn't saw at that moment as active combatants. So we were not 100 per cent, and that is the lead of your question, I think, but we were quite sure that they could not wear anything, but it was a possibility -- the possibility was that they could conceal something, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Right. In answering questions by my predecessors, they confronted you with a part of your statement where you testified about a wounded fighter, of whom you knew that he was a fighter, but he was wearing civilian clothes. Could we conclude from that that there were members of the BiH army who wore civilian clothes and that what they wore was not reliable in terms of inferring who was civilian and who was military personnel?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: I was -- during my time, a lot of patrolling was done by me and the teams from the Charlie Company, and I knew, personally, a lot of the BiH fighters. Also, this one who was laying in the wheelbarrow. That was the only one that I noticed myself that was among the refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But my question was very specific in terms of the clothes that he was wearing. He was wearing civilian clothes at the time. Shall I rephrase my question? During these proceedings, we've heard testimony of some members of the BiH army who testified that they had worn civilian clothes at the time. Could we elicit from you whether you had a similar experience?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: If we're talking about that specific situation, the man in the wheelbarrow, he was wearing civilian clothes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. At a certain moment, on the 12th of July, buses started arriving and trucks intended to transport the refugees towards Kladanj. Were you there when the first buses and trucks departed or arrived? Did you see their arrival?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: From what I could see at the -- from out of the bus remise, I saw the first arrival of the buses, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: At that time, a large throng of refugees had already arrived there in that part of the compound and the bus remise. Did this crowd of refugees started running towards the buses and trucks in desire to board as soon as possible? Do you remember such an event?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes. They were very eager to leave the place, but there was a reason for it, and I'm noticing that you're getting a little impatient but I'm not. The situation was there was a fire truck bringing water in and there was a van bringing bread in, and there was all kind of things distributed. Those people hadn't been fed for a few days, so that was the reason that they first made their moves towards the bus line or truck line.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Sir, I can promise you we'll come to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're showing patience now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, at a certain point, there was a commotion among the refugees, and some witnesses labelled that situation as a human stampede. My question to you is whether you remember such an occurrence?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. From your vantage point, and that should be the bus remise from your testimony, it could be clearly -- the situation could be clearly said where in a human chain we would have one Serb, one Dutch soldier, holding hands and trying to prevent another human stampede; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: I cannot clarify that, because I saw Dutch soldiers trying to prevent that. Probably also Serb preventing that, but I haven't seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you then exclude the possibility that there would be such a situation where Serb and Dutch soldiers would work together to thwart panic spreading among the refugees by creating such a human chain or a human shield?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No, I cannot exclude it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he has answered you already, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, well, I will continue but my question was whether he can exclude such possibility. Okay. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we coming to the part that you so eagerly anticipated, and that is the arrival of General Mladic to Potocari. You said that he was escorted by Nikolic and an interpreter, that there was a film and TV crew recording events. It is on the -- in the third paragraph on the third page of this version. Did you have occasion to hear and see General Mladic personally, you?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: As you suggested, shall I answer this with yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Please. Whether you saw Mr. Mladic or not?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear him addressing the refugees?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you later, after all these events, watching various documentaries and maybe news coverage of different trials, did you manage to hear what Mladic said to the refugees at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm to us that he said that who wanted to leave could leave, who wanted to stay could stay, that buses had been secured and that whoever wanted to leave would be bussed out to Kladanj? Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes. I've seen such a documentary.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now I would like to tackle the situation where the water tanker and the truck with bread arrived and that bread was then distributed among the refugees. If I understood well your interpretation of this event, and given that the TV crew was filming everything, your conclusion was that the whole show was put on for propaganda purposes, to provide some positive coverage and spin on Mladic's actions. Would this describe your understanding of the event?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: But at a certain point, that bread was distributed, cameras were off, the whole shebang was over and there was no longer a need for that kind of propaganda; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that there is testimony provided by a member of the DutchBat, one of your colleagues, that after all that, quite a long time after that, there was another truck full with bread and that bread was distributed among the refugees, and if I told you that some refugees told us that they had received more bread, would that change your conclusion that you just now expressed?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Right. With your colleagues, a certain number of DutchBat members, you were close to the bus depot or remise, and certain situations emerged where your soldiers had been dispossessed of certain items by Serb soldiers and that you protested this fact to Major Nikolic. Do you recall this?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, I can recall that, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Major Nikolic was escorting General Mladic, according to your testimony; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: You knew Major Nikolic from before. I'm not saying that you were close acquaintances, but you knew who he was before the events of the 11th, 12th and 13th of July, 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, because he was a liaison to the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. Reason why you addressed Major Nikolic to resolve this situation where certain effects, personal effects, were stolen from your soldiers was that he had enough authority to remedy the situation and to prevent such things from happening in the future; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: That is partly correct, because there was also a member of the S5 team, a captain Matthijsen from DutchBat around and I addressed him first and Nikolic stood right next to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. But in your statement, it is said that -- page 3, paragraph 4, this is not very consequential, but I believe it's stated that you protested this with Nikolic. Let us make these things clear, whether you addressed Nikolic or somebody else?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: I spoke in fact to both of them because they were listening both but I addressed in fact, of course, a member of the S5 team because that was the procedure, they had the contacts formally with Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. But generally speaking, was your conclusion such that Mr. Nikolic, had he wanted to, he could obtain the return of those items to your soldiers? Was your impression that he didn't want to?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, that was my impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's broach the 13th of July in the morning issue. You stated that you went to the "White House". We are referring to your first visit to the "White House". You said that personal ID documents were in front of the house in a heap. It is stated in the last paragraph on page 3 of your statement. And after that, you entered the "White House". Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you collect any of those personal documents that you saw in front of the house? Did you take -- pick it up, open it, try to establish what they stood for?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No, because a Serb soldier was around that pile of ID, and it was not -- I felt at that moment it was not very -- not very, how shall I put it, not very convenient to pick it up and then have a close look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Oh, all right, which means that you did not pick up and inspect any of those documents?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No, but they were laying open and it was a clear look on that pile. Some of them were open, some closed. What you actually was seeing that there was different kinds of ID.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, all right. But what I am interested in is specifically one, two or three documents that you may have taken, opened, read the name so that you could testify that such a document would belong to such person. That did not happen, did it?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. At the moment when you entered the "White House" and you spent some time there, you saw a certain number of people captured there. Did you personally know any of those who were kept in the house?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: I knew some boys from patrolling, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us the name of those boys?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Which means that we cannot establish, given that you do not know the persons in there, that you did not compare the documents, we cannot make a connection between the documents outside the house and the people inside the house?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: That is your conclusion. My conclusion is another one, that people -- I've seen people walk into the "White House". Before they walked into the "White House", it was said by Serbs to put their luggage or rucksacks on a big heap. The next step was that they were sent into the house. And along the rucksacks and the big heap of IDs, they were told to throw everything that they did not need any more and then go into the house. So there is, to my opinion, and under my view, was a clear connection about the men who put down the rucksacks and threw out their ID and went into the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Sir, we've heard testimony of DutchBat members, your colleagues, who would find IDs in other locations, in the wider area of Potocari, within the compound itself, outside the base, heaps of different IDs. Can you confirm that for us, please?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No, I cannot confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It's all right. We also heard testimony, from a certain number of witnesses, Muslims, who spoke about them tossing away their IDs to prevent them being identified by Serbian soldiers and that a large number of them did not possess their IDs on their person. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Now, may I ask you about the IDs? What do you refer to under the term "ID"?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Passports, working permits, all kinds of officially -- by any authority given cards, with pass photos on it and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, would it be convenient to take the break at this point, because I'm going to move to the next topic and I cannot finish it by the time for a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. We'll have a 30-minute break now and we will continue. Do you think you will finish your cross-examination today?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I will -- I think I'm in the middle of my cross-examination, so I'll do my best to complete it by the end of today's session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's reduce the break to 25 minutes. That means we will reconvene at 10 minutes to 1.00. Thank you. And we will stop at 1.30 any way. I suppose you are going next?

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Your Honour, there has been an agreement that we would actually go last, but I was just about to say, that given I won't start until Monday, I'm happy to start Monday. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's continue and we stop at 1.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Major Rutten, can we now deal with another subject, and that would be the "White House" that we've heard of and discussed and that you discussed with my learned colleagues during your cross-examination. You said in your statement that two soldiers from the 108 Commando Company stood in front of the "White House"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: For us to gain an impression about all that, these people from the 108 Commando Company, are they UNMO members or DutchBat members?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: They were DutchBat members.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Also, apart from those two members of 108 Commando Company, there were members of UNMO who were observing what was going on in the "White House", I specifically mean Major De Haan that you mentioned; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Major De Haan was at a certain point there, but were not constantly observing the "White House".

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Right. But were there other UNMO members observing the house? Let me be specific in my question. We have a testimony of one of commanders of the DutchBat who, in his testimony, stated that UNMO members had the tasks of counting the number of people entering the house and the number of those leaving the house and as per records, the same number of people entered the house and exited the house while being taken to the busses. Can you confirm that for us, please?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: The only thing I can confirm is that there was an UNMO, an African colleague named Kingori was also around. The other part of your question, I cannot confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. One member of the DutchBat who, just as you did, entered the "White House" but not with you, he stated that in the "White House" he saw a heap of knives, a heap of knives within the "White House" which, according to his testimony, belonged to the Muslims who had been taken in there. When you entered the "White House", did you personally encounter or pass by that heap of knives?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: I've never seen that heap of knives.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. But you must have seen, and this is reflected in your Krstic testimony and in your previous statements, you did see a heap of photographs. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In connection with these photographs, I would like to confront you with what you spoke about before a parliamentary commission in -- during the parliamentary inquiry on the 11th of November, 2002. That is Exhibit 3D39, 10th page. And before we see that on the screen, I would like to quote this, "that on benches on tables for the purpose of establishing whether any of them were known." Do you remember that part of your testimony before the parliamentary commission?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Sorry, I can't read your gish gish in line 6 on 58, 57. Gish gish on benches, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It's page 10, paragraph first. I'm sorry, you're referring to the transcript?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes. I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It starts with the photos of the men were in a line?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: On bed, on benches on tables.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Now I understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Does this refresh your memory? Is this what you saw in the "White House"?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes. That was on the other side of the "White House", the other entrance. We went in that. Together with me was the sergeant major van Schaik and there we witnessed that there were photos laying all around and I stated then that the photos of men being -- of led -- laying next to each other on benches, couches and on tables to identify -- and there were only photos of men, and family photos of other people were laying on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I'm just interested in the conclusion you drew from it because I share the same conclusion, namely, that the purpose of separating the photograph of men being separated and lined up, was done in order to identify the men; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yeah, you could say that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, generally speaking, based on that fact, there was an identification process of men conducted in the "White House", the men who had been taken to the "White House"?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: The problem here is that you're connecting something that took already beforehand in place --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, stop. I don't think it's a fair question, because you're asking him to draw a conclusion and I very much doubt if he can draw a conclusion based on the basic information that you're putting to him. I mean, if he can draw a conclusion of which he is convinced, yes, by all means, go ahead, Major, but if it makes you speculate, then I don't want to you answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, maybe I can reformulate this question and that would be much easier for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By all means, Mr. Lazarevic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you stand by the statement given to the parliamentary commission of the Netherlands on the 11th of November, 2002, the purpose of establishing whether any of them were known?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now I would like to turn to another document, which has already been admitted into evidence. This is document -- Exhibit 4D15. I think it would be very good if we waited for you to see it on the screen. I think that the English translation of this exhibit has not yet arrived, even though it's been admitted a long time ago. I'll just read out the heading of the document following which are just the names. It says here, "The list of war criminals known to the command of the 1st Light Infantry Brigade, which is to say the Bratunac Brigade, who committed war crimes in the territory of Bratunac, Srebrenica, Milici, Vlasenica and Skelani municipalities, concerning whom there are indicia that they are located in Srebrenica." And then, can we see the last page of this document because this document just contains the numbers and names of the people. It says here, "Bratunac, 12th of July, 1995." My first question to you is: Have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of existence of a list of people suspected of having committed war crimes and that it was used as grounds for identifying people from Srebrenica who may have participated in it?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: I heard about a list, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Is that consistent with your experience from the time you spent in Srebrenica, that there was some list based on which the identity of persons from Srebrenica was investigated and established?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: It wasn't -- it was not known by me that there was a connection between those lists and the interrogations that were going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. [In English] Fair enough. [Interpretation] Now, let us continue briefly with the "White House". Based on the information available in this case, and based on the evidence, I must say, of a large number of DutchBat members, on the 12th or 13th of July, 1995, at least six commanding officers of DutchBat entered the "White House". I can give you their names, if you wish. Major Egbers, Boering, Koster, van Duijn, you, yourself, Mr. Rutten, and according to your testimony, also Mr. Van Schaik. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: The only one I can confirm is the NCO, that's not an officer, the warrant officer van Schaik and the other names I wasn't present at that time that they were in the house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: However, did you ever come to know that they entered or they were at the "White House"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard from the Lieutenant van Duijn that he was near the "White House", but I never heard from him that he was in the "White House", yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the other officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And that also reflects the officer Koster.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And Egbers, yes, they were near there but they never told me that they were in the "White House", sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Naturally, I do not insist on you speaking of the things that you didn't see yourself or don't have firsthand knowledge of, but these two members of DutchBat from the 108th commando unit also entered the "White House", didn't they?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: They were -- sorry, yes, they were in the "White House", yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Based on the calculation that I can do myself, at least, eight members of DutchBat entered the "White House" at the time, so this was not something that was concealed from the members of the DutchBat, nor from the UNMO members, the fact that men were being taken to the "White House" and interrogated there.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No. It couldn't be concealed because it was at the opposite side of the road so we could see it very clearly, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That's precisely so. This was unfolding directly across from the UN compound. In addition to that, based on your own testimony, you made a certain number of photographs inside the "White House", didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Nobody stopped you from taking photographs in the "White House"?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: They weren't aware of what I was doing in the first floor of the "White House", at least they -- the Serbs weren't aware of what I was doing there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. But in order for you to take photographs inside the "White House", you had to use a flash. Otherwise, photographs would be useless. Didn't you consider that to be extremely careless and irresponsible for you to expose yourself to so much danger?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: That is my own responsibility, so I can handle that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Are these the photographs which disappeared while being developed here in Holland, these photographs taken inside the "White House"? Are we referring to the same photographs?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So that is the same film containing the photographs of the nine bodies for which you say you found them in a meadow. And were the photographs from inside the "White House" on the same film as the photographs you took from the compound depicting the burning of piles of photographs -- of documents and clothing?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: There is a difference. The first part is correct. So the photographs of the nine bodies. And the photos inside the "White House". The second part is depicting the burning of the piles at the opposite side of the compound. I still have those photos and they were presented in the Krstic case. So that wasn't the same film, the second film that I put in the camera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before I forget, Mr. Lazarevic and Mr. Thayer, just for the record and for formalities' sake, just wanted to confirm that we are sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis at the moment, Judge Kwon being absent for a just cause. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: What else was on that film with the photographs of burning belongings?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Now you're speaking about the second film.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, the second one.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes. Also, there were photographs on it of the looting of houses nearby the compound, Serb civilians leading cattle and carrying wheelbarrows full of personal stuff, what formerly belonged to the Muslim population, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. Again, I can promise you we'll get to this topic. [Interpretation] The night between the 12th and 13th of July, you spent that night inside the Potocari compound base, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We have heard testimonies here, we had exhibits proving this, namely, that during that night, both within the compound and outside of the compound, in the facilities where the refugees were housed, there were several deaths, suicides, a murder of a woman in labour, as well as some other deaths. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: No, I do not personally know about it. Only by hearing it from other colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. That would be sufficient basis for putting my next question to you. So you heard from others that there were deaths within the compound in the night between the 12th and the 13th. Do you know where were the bodies of the people who died or committed suicide that night taken?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
utterances.text: One or two I know was known to me that they were buried at the rear side of the compound, and the other ones, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But let me ask you this: In relation to the cases known to you of bodies being buried, do you know anything about the identification procedure? How was it established, the identity of these people, whether they had relatives, cause of death and the fact that they lived and died that night within the compound?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES HENDRIKUS ANTONIUS RUTTEN
